targets.title: Of pandemics, politics, and personality: The role of conscientiousness and political ideology in the sharing of fake news.
targets.evidence_quote:
We therefore reanalyzed their publicly available data (https://osf
.io/ahdsf/) to examine whether conscientiousness inﬂuences overall
sharing or sharing discernment. We also ran ﬁve new preregistered
studies that aimed to conceptually replicate Lawson and Kakkar’s
(2022) ﬁndings.
targets.outcome_quote:
Our studies were conceptual replications
and differed from the original studies in several ways (see Tables
1 and 2), but we also included a very close replication (Study 5;
only difference is that we used more “up-to-date” headlines). We
did not ﬁnd evidence for the central claims made in their article in
any of our ﬁve studies.
targets.outcome_computational_quote:
Our reanalysis of their data replicated their reported ﬁndings: The negative conservatism–conscientiousness interaction effect was signiﬁcant in all their studies
(Figure 1).
targets.outcome_robustness_quote:
That is,
Lawson and Kakkar’s (2022) ﬁndings pertain to overall sharing
rates (of true and false news), but not speciﬁcally to false news headlines or sharing discernment (i.e., difference in sharing between true
and false news).
targets.outcome_reasoning: All five new-sample conceptual replications failed the central interaction claim. The paper additionally reproduces original-data interaction results but challenges their specificity to misinformation; both axes are retained to describe that component.

reasoning: Mixed design: five new-data replications plus reanalysis of the same single original paper. Primary type follows new-sample studies; reproduction axes separately preserve the original-data component. Reanalysis studies are explicitly identified in Table 1.
